newsitem.title: HAITI: Haitian premier, facing unrest over policy, quits.
newsitem.headline: Haitian premier, facing unrest over policy, quits.

text.p: Haitian Prime Minister Rosny Smarth resigned on Monday after months of criticism of government economic policies that have sparked violent unrest in the poverty-stricken nation.
Smarth's announcement in parliament means President Rene Preval must appoint a new prime minister, who will then name a new cabinet.
"The government has not responded to the needs of the people. The image in certain sectors is no good and the government does not inspire confidence," Smarth said.
"And about the political plan, I don't agree with the way the game is being played, without principle, without ethics. For that reason, I think it is time that another team takes the reins," he said.

President Rene Preval, who was not in parliament when Smarth spoke, appointed the former agricultural economist as premier 15 months ago as a huge international effort got under way to help the country recover from several years of brutal military rule.

But in recent months Smarth has been the focus of general strikes and violent demonstrations by grassroots organisations that oppose a government economic plan guided by the International Monetary Fund and foreign donors.
It includes the privatisation of nine state enterprises but opponents say it is only aggravating poverty in Haiti, already the poorest country in the Americas.
In mid-May, mobs demanding Smarth's resignation burned cars and tires and exchanged gunfire with police as student demonstrations flared into two days of general rioting.
U.S. officials, reacting to Smarth's move, said the government must maintain the same direction.

"We look forward to developing a good working relationship with Mr. Smarth's successor after he or she is nominated by President Preval and confirmed by the Haitian Parliament. We hope that this process is completed in a manner which maintains the momentum of the Haitian goverment's economic reform efforts," U.S. Embassy spokeswoman Meg Gilroy said.
Earlier on Monday, Haitian radio broadcast strong criticism by former president Jean-Bertrand Aristide of government programmes.

"It is a game of organising their own business rules which are good for those that have more, and bad for those that have less. For (the international community) it is them first, them next, and them in the end," Aristide said in his strongest criticism yet of the programmes.
In his speech on Monday, Smarth criticised local elections held in April and the Provisional Electoral Council, saying there were irregularities and important votes had not been counted.

Candidates from a new party formed by Aristide won two of nine seats out of 27 in the Senate that were up for grabs. Runoff elections for the seven seats are scheduled for June 15. If Aristide's Famni Lavalas takes control of Parliament, key laws for a structural adjustment plan may not be passed.

Aristide, a charismatic priest who championed Haiti's poor, was elected president in 1990 after almost 30 years of repressive dictatorship. After eight months he was ousted in a military coup and forced into exile.
A U.S.-led military intervention paved the road for his return in 1994. The next year he handed over power to Preval but the two have since fallen out over policy.

Smarth was never popular with Haiti's impoverished masses. He enraged residents of Cite Soleil, a vast slum on the edge of the capital, when he visited last November after fires burned down many hundreds of houses. Wearing a crisp suit, he held his nose as he walked through its sewage-stained streets.
